'''Wembury''' is a village on the south coast of [[Devon]], England, very close to [[Plymouth Sound]]. Wembury is located south of Plymouth. Wembury is also the name of the [[peninsula]] in which the village is situated. The village lies in the administrative district of the [[South Hams]] within the [[South Devon Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty]] (AONB). The [[South West Coast Path]] goes past the coastal end of the town. The [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] has taken an active role in maintaining the scenic and historic characteristics of the village and its surrounding area

The beach is well known for its surfing and rock pooling. [[Wembury Marine Centre]] educates visitors about what they can find in the rockpools and how they can help protect and preserve them. The centre is managed by [[Devon Wildlife Trust]] and was refurbished in 2006.  [[Basking sharks]] can be seen in the summer near the Mewstone. There is also Wembury primary school.

There are three pubs within the Wembury parish; the Eddystone Inn, Mussell Inn and the Odd Wheel (the Oddy). Three shops are also in Wembury.

Its [[electoral ward]] is called 'Wembury and Brixton'. The ward population at the [[United Kingdom Census 2011|2011 census]] was 4,455.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ukcensusdata.com/wembury-and-brixton-e05003586#sthash.cJrYV5rv.dpbs|title=Ward population 2011|access-date= 20 February 2015}}</ref>

== History ==
Wembury was visited by [[Mesolithic]] man as evidenced by flint implements found on local sites. Some [[Ancient Rome|Roman]] coins have also been found.

The name ''Wembury'' may derive from a place name containing the name [[Woden]],<ref>'Report and transactions, Volume 10'.Devonshire  Association for the Advancement of Science 1878. Original from the University of California. Pages 285, 299</ref><ref name=ISAAC>Taylor, Isaac. 'Words and Places: or, Etymological Illustrations of History, Ethnology, and Geography'. Macmillan, 1865, Harvard University. {{ISBN|1-4212-7015-3}} Length: 561 pages. Pages 322 and 323</ref><ref name=ALLEN>Allen, Grant.'Early Britain' BiblioBazaar, LLC, 2007. {{ISBN|1-4346-0560-4}}, {{ISBN|978-1-4346-0560-3}}. Length: 172 pages. Page 63</ref> and John Mitchell Kemble notes that it was called {{lang|ang|Wódnesbeorh}}.<ref name=KEMB>Kemble, John Mitchell. de Gray Birch, John (editor). 'The Saxons in England V1: A History of the English Commonwealth Till the Period of the Norman Conquest'. Longman, Brown, Green & Longmans, 1849. {{ISBN|978-1-4326-3740-8}}. Length: 562 pages. Page 336, 343, 344</ref>

Saxons colonised south-west Devon during the 7th century and founded agricultural settlements here. There was also a church dedicated to [[Saint Werburgh]], a [[Anglo-Saxons|Saxon]] saint, in the area, an alternative derivation for the name.

Wembury expanded vastly in the 20th century with areas of farmland sold off for housing. Some older buildings are still present in the village, mainly in Knighton and West Wembury.

== Wembury in the public eye ==
Wembury is mentioned in ''The [[Forsyte Saga]]'' by [[John Galsworthy]]. Galsworthy visited Wembury as part of his research for the book, he was intensely interested in his own origins and descent through a long line of Devon farmers who farmed in Wembury for three hundred years from the 17th century to the late 19th century.

Wembury was used as a location in the filming of the [[The Comic Strip|Comic Strip]]'s parody ''[[Five Go Mad on Mescalin]]''. In the film the Mewstone can be clearly seen.
[[File:Wembury,_St_Werburgh's_church_and_Wembury_beach_-_geograph.org.uk_-_613411.jpg|St Werburgh's Church Above the beach|right|thumb]] 
[[File:Wembury from the sea.jpg|Heybrook Bay, Wembury parish, from the sea|right|thumb]]

== Wembury parish ==
[[File:WemburyHouse Devon 1797 ByRevJohnSwete.jpg|thumb|200px|1797 watercolour by Rev. [[John Swete]] (d.1821) of the ruins of Wembury House, built by Sir John Hele]]
The [[parish]] of Wembury was once divided into four [[Manorialism|manor]]s: Wembury, [[Down Thomas]], [[Langdon, Devon|Langdon]] and Alfelmeston. According to Lyson's ''Devonshire'', published in 1822, the manor of Wembury originally belonged to [[Plympton Priory]]. After the [[dissolution of the monasteries]] in 1539 it went into private ownership.

Today the parish of Wembury is divided into three principal villages; Wembury, [[Down Thomas]], and [[Heybrook Bay]]. There are also a number of smaller hamlets; Hollacombe, Knighton, Thorn, Langdon, Andurn and Bovisand. The population of the parish was 2740 during the 2011 census.

Wembury House survives as an elegant late [[Georgian architecture|Georgian]] mansion, originally an exceptionally grand [[Elizabethan architecture|Elizabethan]] house built by the lawyer Sir [[John Hele (died 1608)|John Hele]] (c.1541–1608) a [[Member of Parliament]] for [[Exeter (UK Parliament constituency)|Exeter]] and [[Recorder of Exeter]] (1592–1605). It was already a ruin by about 1700,<ref>[[Todd Gray (Devon Historian)|Gray, Todd]] & Rowe, Margery (Eds.), Travels in Georgian Devon: The Illustrated Journals of The Reverend [[John Swete]], 1789-1800, 4 vols., Tiverton, 1999, Vol.4, p.6: Swete writing in 1797 referred to "Wembury the ruinous house" and its "magnificence about a century ago"</ref> and was finally demolished in 1803.<ref>[[William George Hoskins|Hoskins, W.G.]], A New Survey of England: Devon, London, 1959 (first published 1954), p.513</ref>
The surviving house on the site was built in the early 19th century and rebuilt by [[Major Edmund Lockyer]].

Fort Bovisand, an ancient monument lies in the North West corner of the parish. The first fort on this site was built in 1845. Plans have been approved for the conversion of Bovisand Fort and associated buildings, removal of one building, and construction of new towers, an apartment building, 11 new dwellings, new quayside commercial accommodation and conservation of historic fabric, together with associated landscaping, parking and re-establishment of the link to the coastal footpath, creating a total of 81 residential units, office, teaching/studio space, event space, visitor centre and facilities, café and relocation of MOD space and additional commercial space.

== The Mewstone ==
A distinctive feature visible from Wembury Beach is the Mewstone, a triangular island which is uninhabited. In the past it has been host to a prison and a private home, as well as a refuge for local [[smugglers]]. Its most infamous resident was Sam Wakeman who, in 1744,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://salcombe-art.com/tag/sam-wakeman|title=Sam Wakeman Archives}}</ref> avoided transportation to Australia in favour of the cheaper option of transportation to the Mewstone, where he was interned for seven years.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Gardner|first1=Suze|title=The A-Z of Curious Devon|date=2016|publisher=The History Press|isbn=9780750964104|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VSiUCwAAQBAJ&q=Wembury+Mewstone+Sam+Wakeman&pg=PT176}}</ref> After his internment on the island he remained there paying his rent by supplying rabbits for the Manor House table. It is said Sam Wakeman is responsible for carving the rough stone steps to the summit of the Mewstone.<ref>{{cite web|title=Wembury Beach - Wembury|url=http://www.southhams.com/directory/wembury-beach-wembury-131.html|publisher=South Hams|access-date=10 July 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=The Mewstone|url=http://www.wemburyparishcouncil.info/Core/wemburypc/UserFiles/Files/themewstone-2.pdf|publisher=Wembury Parish Council|access-date=10 July 2016}}</ref>

The island was painted several times by [[J. M. W. Turner]] after sketching it during a sailing trip from Plymouth in 1813. ''The Mewstone'', painted between 1823 and 1826, was left to the nation by the [[Turner Bequest]] and is in the collection of [[Tate Britain]]. A [[watercolour]] of about 1814 in the [[National Gallery of Ireland]], [[Dublin]] is entitled ''The Mew Stone, at the Entrance of Plymouth Sound, Devonshire''. Another watercolour traditionally known as ''Storm off Margate'' in a private collection, is now accepted to be a view of The Mewstone.<ref>[http://www.tate.org.uk/art/artworks/turner-the-mewstone-d17170 Tate - Art and artists - Joseph Mallord William Turner, The Mewstone c.1823-6]</ref> A further Turner painting that had been identified as the [[Bass Rock]] in the [[Firth of Forth]] was re catalogued as The Mewstone when it was auctioned by [[Christie's]] in 2008.<ref>[http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/england/devon/7431173.stm BBC News - Monday, 2 June 2008 - Fine art experts in Turner U-turn]</ref>

The Great Mewstone and Little Mewstone are now a bird sanctuary and access is not permitted to visitors.

3978476.title: River Heddon
3978476.extract:
The River Heddon is a river in Devon, in the south of England. Running along the western edges of Exmoor, the river reaches the North Devon coast at Heddon's Mouth. The nearest road access to the beach is at Hunter's Inn, approximately 1.6-kilometre (1 mi) south of sea-fall. The named river flows for 8.8 kilometres (5.5 mi) and drains an area of 17.07 square kilometres (6.59 sq mi).
The Heddon Valley is renowned for its natural environment, with bridges and stepping stones along the river, meadows, and walks which start from the National Trust shop and information centre which has been in the ownership of the National Trust since 1963.
The cobbled beach at Heddon's Mouth is approximately 300 metres (980 ft) wide and is only accessible through footpaths on the National Trust land or via the South West Coast Path.  There are remains of a lime kiln on its western edge. The valley immediately landwards of the beach has steep slopes to its east and west, with the hills climbing over 200 metres (660 ft) in altitude within 500 metres (1,600 ft) of the river. The remains of a Roman fortlet are visible on the hilltop to the east of Heddon's Mouth.
The Lynton & Barnstaple Railway once ran through part of the valley, halting at the small village of Parracombe.

4007204.title: Killerton
4007204.extract:
Killerton is an 18th-century house in Broadclyst, Exeter, Devon, England, which, with its hillside garden and estate, has been owned by the National Trust since 1944 and is open to the public. The National Trust displays the house as a comfortable home. On display in the house is a collection of 18th- to 20th-century costumes, originally known as the Paulise de Bush collection, shown in period rooms.
The estate covers some 2,590 hectares (25.9 km2, 6,400 acres). Included in the estate is a steep wooded hillside with the remains of an Iron Age hill fort on top of it, known as Dolbury, which has also yielded evidence of Roman occupation, namely a triple-ditched Roman fort or marching camp which is still visible in aerial photographs, despite heavy ploughing within the hill fort.
Killerton House itself and the Bear's Hut summerhouse in the grounds are Grade II* listed buildings. The gardens are Grade II* listed in the National Register of Historic Parks and Gardens.

'''Killerton''' is an 18th-century house in [[Broadclyst]], [[Exeter]], [[Devon]], England, which, with its hillside [[garden]] and estate, has been owned by the [[National Trust]] since 1944 and is open to the public. The National Trust displays the house as a comfortable home. On display in the house is a collection of 18th- to 20th-century costumes, originally known as the Paulise de Bush collection, shown in period rooms.

The estate covers some 2,590 hectares (25.9 km<sup>2</sup>, 6,400 acres).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/killerton/ |title=National Trust - Killerton |work=web page |publisher=National Trust |access-date=21 April 2012}}</ref> Included in the estate is a steep wooded hillside with the remains of an [[Iron Age]] [[hill fort]] on top of it, known as [[Dolbury]], which has also yielded evidence of Roman occupation, namely a triple-ditched Roman fort or marching camp which is still visible in aerial photographs, despite heavy ploughing within the hill fort.<ref>R.R.Sellman; Aspects of Devon History, Devon Books 1985 - {{ISBN|0-86114-756-1}} - Chapter 2; The Iron Age in Devon. Map Page 11 of Iron Age hill forts in Devon includes Dolbury.</ref>

Killerton House itself and the Bear's Hut summerhouse in the grounds are Grade II* [[listed building]]s.<ref>{{NHLE| num= 1098331| desc= KILLERTON HOUSE AND HA HA APPROXIMATELY 20 METRES IN FRONT OF ENTRANCE |access-date= 8 June 2014}}</ref><ref>{{NHLE| num = 1170706| desc=  THE BEAR'S HUT 220 METRES NORTH NORTH WEST OF KILLERTON HOUSE |access-date= 8 June 2014|fewer-links=yes}}</ref> The gardens are Grade II* listed in the [[National Register of Historic Parks and Gardens]].<ref name="NHLE1000694">{{NHLE |num=1000694 |desc=Killerton House |access-date=12 February 2016 |fewer-links=yes}}</ref>

==History==
[[File:2008-06-26 Killerton Chapel.jpg|thumb|left|Killerton Chapel, which is grade I listed<ref>[https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1098332 Historic England] Chapel of the Holy Evangelists</ref>]]
The manor of [[Columbjohn]] in the parish of [[Broadclyst]] was purchased by Sir [[John Acland (Devon MP)|John Acland]], MP and [[High Sheriff of Devon]]. Shortly afterwards, in 1612, the adjoining estate of Killerton was purchased by his nephew Sir [[Arthur Acland (died 1610)|Arthur Acland]] of [[Acland, Landkey|Acland]] in the parish of [[Landkey]].<ref>[[John Lambrick Vivian|Vivian, Lt.Col. J.L.]], (Ed.) The Visitations of the County of Devon: Comprising the Heralds' Visitations of 1531, 1564 & 1620, Exeter, 1895, p.307, pedigree of Drewe</ref><ref>Acland, Anne, A Devon Family: The Story of the Aclands. London and Chichester: Phillimore, 1981, pp.4-6</ref> The present Georgian Killerton House was built by [[Sir Thomas Acland, 7th baronet]], in 1778. The chapel was built in 1738 to the designs of [[Charles Robert Cockerell]].{{citation needed|date=February 2024}}

The garden was created in the 1770s by [[John Veitch (horticulturist)|John Veitch]], one of the leading [[landscape design]]ers of the time. It features [[rhododendron]]s, [[magnolia]]s, [[herbaceous border]]s and rare trees, as well as an [[Ice house (building)|ice house]] and early 19th-century [[summer house]]. The surrounding parkland and woods offer several circular walks. Plans attributed to [[William Sawrey Gilpin]] (1762-1843) for a new drive from Killerton to Columbjohn (1820) were not implemented.<ref name="NHLE1000694"/> A short play about the meeting between Veitch and Gilpin was commissioned by the [[National Trust]] to be performed in the gardens of Killerton in mid 2016.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/events/83e8693f-e34a-4161-a7a3-52aad5b8f9b6/pages/details |title=ParkLife drama {{!}} National Trust |website=www.nationaltrust.org.uk |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160625124850/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/events/83e8693f-e34a-4161-a7a3-52aad5b8f9b6/pages/details |archive-date=2016-06-25}}</ref>

Killerton was given to the National Trust by the British politician Sir [[Richard Acland]], 15th Baronet in 1944,<ref name="NTHistory">{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/killerton/features/-johnsons-elegance-and-simplicity-of-killerton|title=The history of Killerton House|publisher=National Trust|access-date=13 September 2022}}</ref> and in September 2015 the National Trust commissioned a short drama to be staged on the site entitled ''The Gift'', written by Eileen Dillon, telling the story of Sir Richard's decision to hand over his estate.{{citation needed|date=February 2024}}

==Lost house==
In 2016 an archaeological dig discovered what is believed to be a footprint of an intended replacement home to the current Killerton. Reports believe that this is what has been known in history as the lost house of Devon, of 240 years, designed by architect [[James Wyatt]]. It is within the grounds a shortish walk from the current site, and its existence was obscured by a [[copse]] that looks to have been deliberately planted to hide it.{{Citation needed|date=February 2024}}

The National Trust has placed woodwork in the four corners of what is believed would have been the corners of the intended property. They have also placed a door and frame on what they believe would have been the entrance to the intended billiard room. Killerton's information boards on the site state that there is an intention for further archaeological digs in the future.<ref>{{cite web|title=Volunteering in very special places Volunteer, Killerton|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/profiles/volunteering-in-very-special-places|publisher=National Trust|access-date=5 July 2016}}</ref>

5207359.title: Overbeck's
5207359.extract:
Overbeck's Garden at Sharpitor is an Edwardian 2.75 hectare (7 acre) subtropical Grade II registered garden at Sharpitor, Salcombe, Devon, England. It is named after its last private owner Otto Christop Joseph Gerhardt Ludwig Overbeck (1860–1937).
The original house on the site was "Sharpitor", a small villa by Salcombe builder Albert Stumbles. In 1901 it was bought by Edric Hopkins, who also bought a further 2 acres (8,100 m2) of land, and laid out the garden, creating terraces and planting exotic specimens on the sheltered site. In 1913 the property was bought by Mr and Mrs George Medlicott Vereker who demolished the original house and had the present one built. Otto Overbeck acquired the house in 1928 and lived there until his death in 1937. Wishing the house to be used after his death as "a public park and museum and a Hostel for Youth" Overbeck bequeathed it to the National Trust or Salcombe Urban District Council on condition it be used as such and not as a brothel as so many properties in the surrounding area had become. It was accepted by the National Trust.
Until 2014 the house was divided between a museum and a youth hostel. The youth hostel closed in 2014 when the agreement between the National Trust and the Youth Hostels Association ended. The museum closed in 2020 when the house was shut for repair and maintenance work. The National Trust aims to start re-opening part of the house in 2026.

'''Overbeck's Garden at Sharpitor<ref>{{cite web |title=Overbeck's Garden at Sharpitor |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/devon/overbecks-garden |publisher=National Trust |access-date=1 July 2024}}</ref>''' is an [[Edwardian architecture|Edwardian]] 2.75 hectare (7 acre) subtropical [[Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of Special Historic Interest in England|Grade II registered garden]]<ref>{{cite web |title=Overbecks (Sharpitor) |url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1000697?section=official-list-entry |publisher=Historic England |access-date=1 July 2024}}</ref> at Sharpitor, [[Salcombe]], Devon, England. It is named after its last private owner [[Otto Overbeck|Otto Christop Joseph Gerhardt Ludwig Overbeck]] (1860–1937).

The original house on the site was "Sharpitor", a small villa by Salcombe builder Albert [[Stumbles (surname)|Stumbles]]. In 1901 it was bought by Edric Hopkins, who also bought a further {{convert|2|acre|m2}} of land, and laid out the garden, creating terraces and planting exotic specimens on the sheltered site. In 1913 the property was bought by Mr and Mrs George Medlicott Vereker<ref>{{cite web |title=History of Overbecks |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/devon/overbecks-garden/history-of-overbecks |publisher=National Trust |access-date=1 July 2024}}</ref> who demolished the original house and had the present one built. [[Otto Overbeck]] acquired the house in 1928 and lived there until his death in 1937. Wishing the house to be used after his death as "a public park and museum and a Hostel for Youth" Overbeck bequeathed it to the [[National Trust]] or Salcombe Urban District Council on condition it be used as such and not as a brothel as so many properties in the surrounding area had become.<ref>"Around and About Salcombe", Chips Barber, {{ISBN|978-1-903585-32-0}}</ref><ref>"The History of [[Kingsbridge]] And Salcombe", Anne Born, {{ISBN|978-1-898964-49-0}} (p162)</ref> It was accepted by the National Trust.

Until 2014 the house was divided between a museum and a [[Youth Hostels Association (England & Wales)|youth hostel]]. The youth hostel closed in 2014 when the agreement between the National Trust and the Youth Hostels Association ended. The museum closed in 2020 when the house was shut for repair and maintenance work. The National Trust aims to start re-opening part of the house in 2026.<ref>{{cite web|title=Overbeck’s House closure|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/devon/overbecks-garden/overbecks-house-closure|website=National Trust|access-date=24 September 2025}}</ref>

== Museum ==

The museum displayed some of Overbeck's inventions and collections of stuffed animals, and exhibitions of model sailing ships and various nautical and shipbuilding tools and effects. Many of the maritime-related items have subsequently been displayed at Salcombe Maritime Museum. A room in the middle of the house, one of whose entrances is a "secret" door concealed in the wooden panelling of the room outside, contained a display of dolls' houses, amongst which was "Fred the friendly ghost" for children to discover.<ref>{{cite web|title=The museum at Overbeck's|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/overbecks/features/the-museum-at-overbecks|publisher=National Trust|accessdate=8 July 2016}}</ref> The museum contained a [[Polyphon]] — a large [[musical box]] which played music encoded as holes punched in large sheet-metal discs. There was a collection of discs of popular Edwardian melodies which were played for visitors when the garden was open. There was also a collection of photographs by Edward Chapman who worked in and photographed Salcombe – including the building of the first house on the site – during the early 20th century.

== Garden ==
The garden, begun by Edric Hopkins, was developed by the property's subsequent owners. It has become a specialised collection of tender Mediterranean and Australasian plants growing in the microclimate on the edge of the [[Kingsbridge Estuary]]. The National Trust identify the following separate gardens:.<ref>{{cite web |title=Discover Overbeck's garden |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/devon/overbecks-garden/things-to-see-and-do-at-overbecks-garden |publisher=National Trust |access-date=1 July 2024}}</ref>
* Gazebo Garden
* Statue Garden - formerly the tennis court
* Old Quarry - source of the stone for the house
* Olive Grove
* Banana Garden - the bananas produce fruit most years
* Terraces
* Orange Tree Store - a glasshouse for overwintering the orange tree
* [[Woodland garden|Woodland Garden]]

More detailed information about the history of the garden and its gardeners is given in [https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1000697?section=official-list-entry Historic England's official listing].

The '''Lyd''' is a [[river]] rising at Lyd Head<ref name=OSOL28 /> (Corn Ridge in NW Dartmoor) in the [[Dartmoor]] national park in [[Devon]] in [[South West England]] and flowing into the [[River Tamar]] beyond [[Lifton, Devon|Lifton]].<ref name=OS112 /> It runs through '''Lydford Gorge''', the deepest [[gorge]] in South West England.

==Lydford Gorge==
[[File:Lydford Gorge (detail).jpg|thumb|left|Lydford Gorge (detail)]]
Lydford Gorge ([[National Trust]]) is a dramatic feature of the river at Lydford on the edge of the [[Dartmoor National Park]]; it is a {{convert|1.5|mile|adj=on}} [[gorge]] near [[Lydford]] on the River Lyd, which is the deepest in South West England. It was formed by the process of [[river capture]], where the start of a nearby river eroded backwards until its origin met the Lyd, diverting its course into the second channel.<ref name=DCC />

Owned and maintained by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] since 1947, the gorge features the {{convert|100|ft|adj=on}} tall White Lady [[Waterfall]] and a series of [[whirlpool]]s known as the Devil's Cauldron.<ref name=BBC />

=== Protected area ===
Lydford Gorge is designated as a [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]] (SSSI)<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=SSSI detail |url=https://designatedsites.naturalengland.org.uk/SiteDetail.aspx?SiteCode=S1001022&SiteName=lydford%20gorge&countyCode=&responsiblePerson=&SeaArea=&IFCAArea= |access-date=2025-08-04 |website=designatedsites.naturalengland.org.uk}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Protected Planet {{!}} Lydford Gorge |url=https://www.protectedplanet.net/136959 |access-date=2025-08-04 |website=Protected Planet}}</ref> because of its complex geology and also because of the [[moss]] and [[liverwort]] species recorded here.

==== Biology ====
Ancient woodland is found on the valley sides of the gorge where tree species include [[Quercus robur|pedunculate oak]], [[Fraxinus excelsior|ash]], [[Corylus avellana|hazel]] and [[Ilex aquifolium|holly]]. Herbaceous woodland species include [[Anemonoides nemorosa|wood anemone]], [[Galium odoratum|woodruff]], [[Hyacinthoides non-scripta|bluebell]] and [[Vaccinium myrtillus|bilberry]]. In wet areas, [[Chrysosplenium oppositifolium|opposite-leaved golden saxifrage]] has been recorded.<ref name=":0" /> 

[[Moss]] species include ''[[Mnium stellare]]'' and ''[[Isothecium holtii]]'' (genus ''[[Isothecium]]'')''.'' [[Liverwort]] species include ''[[Trichocolea tomentella]].'' [[Lichen]] species include ''[[Sticta canariensis|Sticta dufourii]]'' that occurs on damp rocks.<ref name=":0" />

Bird species in this protected area include [[Common raven|raven]], [[Common buzzard|buzzard]], [[wood warbler]], [[grey wagtail]] and [[White-throated dipper|dipper]]. [[Eurasian otter|Otters]] have been recorded in the river Lyd.<ref name=":0" />

==== Geology ====
Rock strata exposed in Lydford gorge include different layers of [[slate]] from the [[Devonian]] period including the ''Liddaton Formation'' and the ''Whitelady Formation''.<ref name=":0" /> Thrusts during the [[Variscan orogeny]] have caused major dislocations in the rock successions here.[https://ussher.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/journal/1981/Isaac_1981.pdf]

'''Morte Point''' is a [[peninsula]] on the north west coast of [[Devon]], [[England]], belonging to the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]]. To the east is the village of [[Mortehoe]] and to the south is the seaside resort of [[Woolacombe]].

In the summer season, tractor and trailer rides are operated from the Mortehoe Heritage Centre onto the point for visitors to view the seals that live on the northern side.

==History==
Morte Point (literally meaning death-point) is notorious for being the site of many shipwrecks. Five ships were wrecked in the winter of 1852 alone; [[Bull Point Lighthouse]] was built just 1¼ miles (2 km) north east of the point.<ref name=mccloy27>McCloy, A. and Whitehorne, S. ''Coastal Walks Around Britain'', New Holland, 2009, p.27</ref> One shipwreck, a ship carrying a cargo of live pigs, gave a small cove to the south of the point the name of Grunta Beach (most of the pigs survived; one is supposed to have lived wild on [[seaweed]] for a year).<ref name="mccloy27"/> The [[Royal National Lifeboat Institution]] built a [[Lifeboat (rescue)|lifeboat]] station at Morte Bay in 1871, although the crews always came from [[Ilfracombe Lifeboat Station|the station at Ilfracombe]] on a carriage when the boat was needed. It proved difficult to launch into strong winds blowing onto its west-facing beach and so the station was closed in May 1900.<ref>{{cite book |last= Leach |first= Nicholas |title= Devon's Lifeboat Heritage |year= 2009 |publisher= Twelveheads Press |location= Chacewater |isbn=978- 0-906294-72-7 |page=45 }}</ref>

'''Loughwood Meeting House''' is a historic [[Baptist]] [[chapel]], {{convert|1|mi}} south of the village of [[Dalwood]], [[Devon]] in  England.<ref name="Greeves"/> There was a meeting house on this site in 1653, although the current building may date from the late 17th century or early 18th century. It is one of the earliest surviving Baptist meeting houses. Since 1969 it has been owned by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]].<ref name="Pastscape"/> [[English Heritage]] have designated it a Grade II* [[listed building]].<ref name=EH>{{NHLE |num=1333577  |desc=Loughwood Chapel |accessdate=11 June 2014 }}</ref>

== Origins ==
The meeting house was founded by the Baptists of [[Kilmington, Devon]], a village {{convert|1|mi}} away to the southeast. Prior to the [[Act of Toleration 1689]], the meeting house was illegal, but its location made it suitable as a refuge. It was built into a hillside, at that time surrounded by woodland and accessible only by narrow paths.<ref name="Greeves"/> Furthermore, it lay within a [[exclave|detached outlier]] of the county of [[Dorset]], as the parish of [[Dalwood]] belonged to Dorset until 1842.<ref name="Billing"/> From the outside it resembled a farm-worker's cottage apart from the gravestones surrounding it. It is still used for worship twice a year by the congregation of nearby Kilmington Baptist Church.<ref name=Seventeenth/>

== Architecture ==
The building is of stone rubble with [[buttress]]es and a [[thatch]]ed roof. The interior dates from the mid 18th century to early 19th century.<ref name="Pastscape"/> The interior is set up as a preacher's house with a high pulpit at the centre front. On the left are [[box pew]]s at right angles to the wall, and on the right some are square pews and the others are parallel with the wall. The musicians sat in the front pews of the [[minstrels' gallery|gallery]] where they had their music rests. A notch in the floor was used for the foot of the bass viol. Two small rooms at the back of the meeting house were used for cooking the midday meal when the congregation met on Sundays for the entire day. Outside is the graveyard, the first interment being in 1659, and in the corner of the graveyard is a stable for the horses of those members who had come from far afield.<ref name=Seventeenth>{{cite web |url=http://biblicalstudies.org.uk/pdf/bq/31-4_148.pdf |title=Loughwood Baptists in the Seventeenth Century |author= |date= |publisher=Biblicalstudies.org |accessdate=14 August 2016}}</ref> There was also a [[Baptist beliefs#Believer's baptism|baptismal]] pool.<ref name="Greeves"/>

== Membership ==
The earliest records go back to 1653, but the church had been in existence for some time before that. Two of the earliest members were John Vernon and William Allen who had been part of the victorious Parliamentary forces under [[Thomas Fairfax|General Fairfax]] in the [[English Civil War]] in 1645. Other early members had escaped from France, mostly being [[Huguenot]]s, and because their names were difficult to pronounce, were known as "French". This remains a common surname among church members and in the vicinity.<ref name=Seventeenth/>
